Any quick tips about hardware virtualization that I might not be able to get from the quick search I'm about to do?

VirtualBox is a great starting point, despite being from Oracle. It's free, both in terms of OSS as well as for no charge, at least for a private individual. IIRC there are portions that are not OSS, though, so if you're trying to be a purist, you might want to try other options (I think KVM is a popular one, and I know VMWare is). Be patient with yourself; this is not entirely intuitive unless someone has set everything up for you already. Have a good bit of hard disk space set aside for experimentation, and have Windows ISO's ready (you'll need to boot off of them).

Remember that, unless you set things up specifically to the contrary, anything you save or access will be on your virtual hard disk. You'll have to set up alternate means (e.g. network drives) in order to access drives as you would natively. I believe VirtualBox lets you put together "machine folders," which lets you access directories on the host machine as though they were directories on the virtual machine and vice-versa, but these require pseudo-networking capabilities. Be sure to install the included add-on packages in your virtual machine, as they'll help the process go more smoothly.

Try to start simple with the networking configuration; you can get into trouble with it. If you just want to connect to the Internet through your computer, the defaults will usually work just as well as sticking another machine on your existing networking setup. But you can easily get a lot more fancy than that, and that's not always a good idea. VirtualBox is capable of some neat things with their networking setup - for instance, you can do testing on systems by putting them on a "closed circuit" virtual network where you can have several VMs interacting at once but no leak to the outside world - but you can get yourself in tangles easily if you just go poking at everything you can find because it sounds neat. This is not to scare you off, but it is an encouragement that you should go slowly and carefully.

That said, I have to disagree with the poster above; there ARE performance penalties. However, if you're using hardware-based virtualization, many of these are going to be minimal. Also, the more recent versions supposedly have some sort of telemetry (I'm not sure precisely what that telemetry is; it might very well be harmless, but I haven't found a whole lot of information on the details). IIRC 5.0.x and below should be good, though.

Gaming will probably be problematic. As I understand it, a system that is set up well and has heavy duty hardware can be pretty good for gaming, but you have to know how to set it up (no mean feat). You may also need at least a dedicated GPU specifically for the virtual machine's OS. The support for hardware acceleration, as I understand it, is still experimental, and it has been considered such for years by now.

One thing to note - you can sometimes "fix" problems by just deleting the VM and starting over. Note that this will fuck over any data you had on the virtual machine, not unlike a real machines, but when you're experimenting and don't have anything valuable on it, this is usually the quickest and cleanest way to fix a totally hosed system you don't want to pick at until it works again.

Above all though: DO NOT go activating software you purchased on a virtual machine unless you're sure you're ready to do that; while it gives you great flexibility, you may end up locking your key into a virtual machine, which is fine if you know that you're going to stick with it, but disastrous if you do not in fact stick with it and either screwing it up or deleting it.

My 72 year old mother used it for the last couple of years on one of my Debian spares after her Windows laptop croaked (she got an ipad for Christmas this year, doesn't like it better, but it was a gift). When you're not doing much but netsurfing and email, playing solitaire, and using stuff like ebay it's not that hard to get up to speed on a modern distribution these days.

If your granny only needs to run a browser and type letters in a decent word processor, the unequivocal answer is yes, at least if she's already able to use Windows. Most distros will do a fantastic job of this right out of the box, and if she's using a distro designed for end users and not a whiz-bang, cutting-edge computer, it'll probably make all the right decisions during installation and come up with no problem on the first try. I've been hearing for years about people swapping out broken Windows installs for Ubuntu or Mint for elderly relatives and having fantastic success, and from what I've seen, I believe it.

Things get more complicated from there. Linux is great, but it has some very serious gaps for some markets. These seem to fall into the middle of the spectrum in terms of uses. For complicated uses where you need something heavy-duty and able to keep up with the computer science majors, Linux is great. If you need an appliance where things "just work" or something to run a relatively standard set of applications (specifically a web browsers, LibreOffice, and other "standard" programs in distros) and someone else (specifically the manufacturers) set it up already, Linux is great.

If you want more middle-range desktop work or a light, stupid-simple server, things get more dicey, and you might be in for a rough time if you aren't willing or able to learn (and I do acknowledge there are people who have good reasons not to want to learn Linux).

I run encrypted Linux. What I really wish they would do, is start packing the /boot directory into the encrypted root partition instead of setting it up in plaintext on another partition, which is the default behavior of the installer. I decided to do this because making /boot plaintext is a very bad idea, because if you dual-boot Windows, some Windows malware could mess with the kernel or the initrd since its just sitting there on a plain old ext4 partition.

It is very unlikely because Windows can't read ext4, but some Windows malware author could secretly include ext4 functionality into their program and then screw you over, which they will probably start doing if Linux gets popular enough.

But now that everything is encrypted on this machine except the single Grub sector that boots the Linux environment, it would be WAY more difficult to do. How much malware could you fit into a single sector to compromise the booted Linux instance, and don't forget that you would still need to leave room for the actual boot code!

I guess I'm way off the deep end in paranoia land, but if you can make something more secure and harder to compromise, you should. And Grub2 does support booting encrypted partitions!
